:::{#def-prediction-bias}
#### Bias of a prediction

Let $g$ be a [fitting procedure](#def-fitting-procedure),
and let $\trainset$ be a random [training set](#def-training-set).
At a covariate value $x$,
the prediction $g\paren{x; \trainset}$ is a random variable,
because it depends on the random training data.
The **bias** of the prediction, as a prediction of $\mean(x)$,
is the [bias](estimation.qmd#def-bias) of $g\paren{x; \trainset}$
as an estimator of the [mean function](#def-mean-function) value $\mean(x)$:

$$
\bias{g\paren{x; \trainset}} = \E{g\paren{x; \trainset}} - \mean(x).
$$ {#eq-prediction-bias}

:::

::: {.remark .notes}

In expected prediction error decompositions [@james2021islr2e, Section 2.2.2],
the bias reflects the error introduced by approximating a real-world relationship by a model.

:::

{{< slidebreak >}}

:::{#exm-prediction-bias}
#### Computing the bias of a prediction

Suppose $\mean(x) = 10$,
and the predictions $g\paren{x; \trainset}$,
over repeated training sets,
average $11$.
Then

$$
\begin{aligned}
\bias{g\paren{x; \trainset}} &= 11 - 10 \\
&= 1.
\end{aligned}
$$

The squared bias is $1^2 = 1$,
the value in @exr-epe-three-sources.

:::
